neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person and place, gives the year and season correctly. Assessed with an interpreter using the Punjabi-adapted MoCA: 20/30 with losses in trail-making, digit span backwards, serial subtraction, fluency and delayed recall (2/5 unaided, 4/5 cued). Naming intact in her first language.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Fundi show background diabetic retinopathy with dot-blot haemorrhages and hard exudates. Extraocular movements full, visual fields full. Face symmetric.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk, tone mildly increased in the legs. Strength 5/5 throughout.
neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration absent at the toes and reduced at the ankles; pinprick reduced in a stocking distribution to mid-calf, consistent with diabetic polyneuropathy.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ knees, absent ankle jerks bilaterally, plantar responses flexor.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact in the arms; heel-to-shin limited by sensory loss rather than dysmetria.
neurological_exam.gait: Short-stepped and wide-based with preserved arm swing; she watches the floor while walking. Romberg positive with eye closure. Tandem impossible.
neurological_exam.additional: No tremor, no rigidity. No frontal release signs. Two falls in the past year, both in poor light.

patient.chief_complaint: Two years of forgetfulness and difficulty managing the household, reported by her daughter-in-law
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Harpreet Kaur is a 69-year-old retired seamstress who attends with her daughter-in-law, who interprets. Over two years the family has watched her withdraw from tasks she used to run: she no longer cooks for the household, has twice put salt in the tea, and last winter could not work out how to use the new washing machine although she had used the old one for a decade. Her daughter-in-law is clear that the problem is not language — she has always spoken little Italian — but organisation and speed. She forgets what she was sent to buy but remembers it if reminded of the shop. She is slower in everything and has become quiet. There have been no discrete episodes of weakness, numbness or speech loss. She has fallen twice in the past year, both times in poor light, and her feet have been numb for years. She has had diabetes for twenty-two years with background retinopathy and microalbuminuria and hypertension for twenty. She takes her medication reliably under supervision. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuations, no dream enactment and no tremor. Her thyroid replacement has been stable for eleven years.

mri.impression: Sporadic small-vessel disease of diabetic and hypertensive type: Fazekas 3 confluent white matter hyperintensity with four chronic lacunes and moderately enlarged perivascular spaces, medial temporal lobes preserved. The burden accounts for the cognitive syndrome.

labs.interpretation: HbA1c 8.9% indicates poorly controlled long-standing diabetes. Microalbuminuria at 62 mg/g and eGFR 58 confirm diabetic microvascular disease. TSH 2.6 mIU/L is normal on replacement, excluding hypothyroid cognitive impairment. B12 244 pg/mL is low-normal in a patient on metformin and warrants correction, but is not the explanation. RPR non-reactive, HIV negative.

specialized_test.impression: Using culture-fair instruments administered in Punjabi, the profile is subcortical: impaired set-shifting, processing speed and fluency with preserved recognition memory and visuospatial copy. Neither literacy nor language explains the pattern.

findings.performance: Naming and comprehension intact in Punjabi — spared

clinical_assessment.impression: Punjabi-adapted MoCA 20/30 administered in her first language with a trained interpreter, with the deficit concentrated in executive function, attention and processing speed and recall responsive to cueing. Language is intact in her first language, which excludes a linguistic artefact. Instrumental independence has been lost.

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement
results.authors: Sachdev P, Kalaria R, O'Brien J, et al.
results.summary: Requires a cognitive syndrome documented on a validated instrument plus imaging or temporal evidence that cerebrovascular disease accounts for it.

results.title: Neuroimaging standards for research into small vessel disease (STRIVE-2)
results.authors: Duering M, Biessels GJ, Brodtmann A, et al.
results.summary: Defines and standardises the reporting of white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, perivascular spaces and cortical superficial siderosis.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Vascular dementia — subcortical ischaemic (small-vessel) type on a background of long-standing diabetes and hypertension, with coexisting diabetic polyneuropathy contributing to the gait disorder

differential.key_features: Cue-responsive recall, preserved medial temporal lobes and an executive-predominant profile argue against it

differential.diagnosis: Cognitive impairment misattributed to language and literacy
differential.key_features: Testing was performed in her first language with culture-fair instruments and the deficit persisted, and the informant history documents loss of previously held household competence
B12 244 pg/mL on metformin is low-normal and should be corrected, but it does not explain a Fazekas 3 burden with four lacunes
TSH 2.6 mIU/L on stable replacement excludes it
No fluctuation, hallucinations, parkinsonism or dream enactment

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a collateral history from an informant who sees the patient daily: the shape of the decline (abrupt, stepwise or gradual), whether any step can be dated to a cerebrovascular event, and which instrumental activities have been lost
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Two years of progressive executive and processing-speed decline with loss of household competence, cue-responsive memory, no dateable stroke, and long-standing diabetes and hypertension with microvascular damage already documented in the eye and kidney

optimal_actions.action: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Adapted MoCA 20/30 in her first language with an executive-predominant profile and cue-responsive recall — the deficit is not an artefact of language or literacy

optimal_actions.action: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible causes excluded (TSH normal on replacement); HbA1c 8.9% with microalbuminuria confirms active microvascular disease; low-normal B12 on metformin identified as a contributor to correct

optimal_actions.action: Perform timed gait and balance testing: the short-stepped, wide-based gait with preserved arm swing is part of the subcortical syndrome and separates it from the gait of normal pressure hydrocephalus and of parkinsonian disorders
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Timed-up-and-go 17.2 s with a short-stepped wide-based gait plus a superimposed sensory ataxic component from diabetic neuropathy

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms — FLAIR for white matter hyperintensity with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI to establish that the lesions are chronic, and SWI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — together with the medial temporal atrophy grade
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Fazekas 3 confluent white matter hyperintensity with four chronic lacunes and preserved medial temporal lobes — a small-vessel burden sufficient for the attribution

optimal_actions.action: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Culture-fair, language-appropriate testing confirms the executive-predominant subcortical profile

optimal_actions.action: Confirm the diagnostic criteria applied and the current secondary-prevention targets against the guidelines
optimal_actions.expected_finding: VASCOG 2014 criteria and the 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention targets confirmed

optimal_actions.action: Review the medication list for anticholinergic burden and for the interaction between antithrombotic choice and the microbleed burden before prescribing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticholinergic contributors identified and the antithrombotic choice reconciled with the imaging burden

optimal_actions.action: Intensify diabetic and blood-pressure control toward an HbA1c below 7.5% and a systolic below 130 mmHg, raise the statin to reach an LDL below 70 mg/dL, correct the low-normal B12 in a patient on long-term metformin, and arrange falls prevention addressing both the vascular gait disorder and the neuropathic sensory loss
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Glycaemic, blood-pressure and lipid targets set; B12 corrected; falls risk addressed for both contributing mechanisms

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis and its mechanism to the patient and the informant, and address driving, medication management, finances, advance care planning and caregiver support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and informant engaged in care planning; safety domains addressed

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Assess cognition in the patient's first language with culture-fair instruments before concluding impairment
Obtain an informant history of previously held competences to establish decline from baseline
Exclude reversible causes, including thyroid disease and B12 deficiency in a patient on metformin
Obtain brain MRI with SWI and grade the burden in STRIVE-2 terms
Separate the vascular gait disorder from the neuropathic one, since both are present and both are treatable
Bring glycaemia, blood pressure and lipids to target
Provide family education and caregiver support through the interpreter
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose or exclude dementia on a test administered in a language the patient does not read or speak fluently
Do not prescribe anticholinergic agents in a patient with small-vessel disease and falls risk
Do not attribute the whole gait disorder to diabetic neuropathy and stop investigating
Do not pursue aggressive glycaemic targets that risk hypoglycaemia in an older patient with cognitive impairment
key_reasoning_points: Cognitive testing in a second language systematically overcalls impairment; the fix is first-language and culture-fair instruments, and the deficit here survives that correction
Diabetes drives small-vessel disease directly, and microvascular damage already documented in the retina and the kidney corroborates the same process in the brain

Two gait disorders can coexist: the wide-based low-clearance pattern with dual-task decay is vascular, while visual dependence and a positive Romberg are neuropathic — and each needs its own intervention
Low-normal B12 on long-term metformin should be corrected on its own merits without being promoted to the explanation of the dementia
Glycaemic targets in an older patient with cognitive impairment must be balanced against hypoglycaemia risk, which itself harms cognition

red_herrings.intended_effect: Invites dismissal of the low MoCA as an artefact of language and education
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Assessment in Punjabi with culture-fair instruments and an informant history of lost household competence establishes genuine decline from baseline

red_herrings.data_point: Absent ankle jerks with stocking sensory loss
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attributes the whole gait disorder, and the falls, to diabetic polyneuropathy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Neuropathy contributes the visual dependence and positive Romberg, but the short-stepped wide-based gait with preserved arm swing and dual-task decay is the vascular component and coexists with it

key_educational_points: Cognitive screening must be language- and culture-appropriate or it produces false positives
Diabetic microvascular damage in the eye and kidney supports the same process in the brain
A vascular and a neuropathic gait disorder can coexist and each requires separate management
Metformin-associated low B12 deserves correction without being over-promoted as the cause of dementia
